bibl.title: The neural roots of mathematical expertise
bibl.publisher: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: Amalric and Dehaene's fMRI comparison of expert mathematicians with non-mathematicians, read for what it settles about the relation between mathematics and language in the brain.
span.quote: Amalric and Dehaene ( 1 ) report a detailed investigation into the neuronal origins and consequences of mathematical expertise.

span.label: critique
span.quote: By showing that expert mathematicians do not recruit brain areas associated with language when engaged in mathematical thinking, Amalric and Dehaene ( 1 ) refute the hypothesis that higher level mathematical abilities are grounded in language systems of the brain.

span.label: mathematical expertise
span.quote: Amalric and Dehaene ( 1 ) report a detailed investigation into the neuronal origins and consequences of mathematical expertise.

span.label: review
span.quote: In PNAS, Amalric and Dehaene ( 1 ) report data that significantly advance our understanding of the origins of high-level mathematical abilities.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Acquiring mathematical expertise drives plastic change in ventral visual cortex for formulas and digits, which in turn reorganises responses to other visual categories such as faces
span.quote: These data may suggest that expertise leads to plastic changes in the cortical processing of mathematical formulas and digits, which, in turn, affect the functional organization of other visual categories.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Expertise redirects attention toward domain-relevant information, which could by itself produce the frontoparietal activation differences
span.quote: Put differently, expertise may change the way in which attention is directed to information relevant to the domain of expertise.

span.label: The commentary's own Neurosynth analysis supports the dissociation independently: regions reported alongside the term numerical are largely separate from those reported alongside language
span.quote: This analysis provides support for the finding that the processing of numerical information is (largely) anatomically distinct from the brain circuitry that is thought to underpin linguistic functions.

span.label: The overlap between advanced mathematical reflection and simple calculation is read as evidence that expertise is built on elementary symbolic number circuits rather than separate from them
span.quote: By doing so, the data speak against the notion that basic number concepts have little to do with advanced mathematics and instead suggest a deep connection between rudimentary symbolic number processing and advanced mathematics.

span.label: Expertise may reorganise the ventral visual stream, with gains for formulas and digits accompanied by reduced response to faces
span.quote: These data may suggest that expertise leads to plastic changes in the cortical processing of mathematical formulas and digits, which, in turn, affect the functional organization of other visual categories.

span.label: The commentary's own alternative account: expertise may change where attention goes rather than which systems are recruited, and the design cannot separate the two
span.quote: Put differently, expertise may change the way in which attention is directed to information relevant to the domain of expertise.

span.label: A test is proposed that would separate them - compare mathematicians on mathematics with experts in another field on their own domain
span.quote: To investigate this possibility further, it would be valuable to compare the brain activation of expert mathematicians reflecting on mathematical statements with the brain activation of experts in a nonmathematical domain listening to statements relevant to their subject of expertise.

span.label: The commentary bounds its own conclusion: language may still matter for the acquisition of expertise, or via connectivity rather than direct recruitment.
span.quote: Notwithstanding, it is possible that language may have played a role in the initial acquisition of mathematical expertise or that such a relationship exists at the level of functional connectivity with language areas of the brain rather than through their direct recruitment.

span.label: The evidence discussed is correlational and cannot establish that expertise causes the reported plastic changes.
span.quote: Importantly, as Amalric and Dehaene ( 1 ) acknowledge, such correlational data cannot be used to infer causality.

span.label: The commentary's own caution, echoing the original authors: the expertise-related brain differences are correlational and cannot establish causality
span.quote: Importantly, as Amalric and Dehaene ( 1 ) acknowledge, such correlational data cannot be used to infer causality.

span.label: Genetic differences between the groups are as compatible with the data as expertise-driven plasticity
span.quote: Although it is possible that the acquisition of mathematical expertise leads to such plastic changes, it is equally plausible that genetic differences between expert mathematicians and nonmathematicians affect the organization of the ventral visual stream.

span.label: The refutation of the language hypothesis is qualified in two ways the data cannot reach
span.quote: Notwithstanding, it is possible that language may have played a role in the initial acquisition of mathematical expertise or that such a relationship exists at the level of functional connectivity with language areas of the brain rather than through their direct recruitment.

span.label: Whether the link to elementary number extends to nonsymbolic representations is untested and not implied
span.quote: A connection between symbolic numbers and mathematical expertise in the brain does not necessarily imply that the same is true for nonsymbolic number processing ( 9 ).

span.label: Whether the reorganisation has behavioural consequences is left as an open question
span.quote: For example, does a reduced response to faces translate into poorer face-processing skills among expert mathematicians?

span.label: number processing - symbolic: numerals and written formulas, which the commented study ties to advanced mathematics
span.quote: By doing so, the data speak against the notion that basic number concepts have little to do with advanced mathematics and instead suggest a deep connection between rudimentary symbolic number processing and advanced mathematics.

span.label: number processing - nonsymbolic: quantity as in dot arrays, shared with other species, and explicitly NOT covered by the result
span.quote: It remains to be investigated whether this connection also extends to nonsymbolic (e.g., comparison of dot arrays) brain representations of numbers that humans share with other species ( 8 ).

span.label: expertise effect - domain-general: attention, working memory and difficulty, which the frontoparietal network also serves
span.quote: It is well established that the frontoparietal brain regions found to be engaged by expert mathematicians are associated with numerous cognitive processes that are not specific to mathematics, such as working memory, attention, and task difficulty ( 12 ).

span.label: expertise effect - domain-specific: information processing particular to the domain, which is the reading the commented paper needs and the design cannot yet secure
span.quote: Such an investigation would help to dissociate effects of expertise on domain-general brain networks of attention from expertise effects on domain-specific information-processing systems in the brain.

span.label: the language claim - Hurford's strong form: numeracy is impossible without language
span.quote: Hurford famously stated: “without language, no numeracy” (ref. 7 , p. 305).

span.label: the language claim - the surviving weak forms: language may matter for ACQUIRING expertise, or through connectivity rather than recruitment
span.quote: Notwithstanding, it is possible that language may have played a role in the initial acquisition of mathematical expertise or that such a relationship exists at the level of functional connectivity with language areas of the brain rather than through their direct recruitment.

span.label: builds-on → Amalric & Dehaene, "Origins of the brain networks for advanced mathematics in expert mathematicians" (PNAS 2016) - the companion article this piece comments on
span.quote: Amalric and Dehaene ( 1 ) report a detailed investigation into the neuronal origins and consequences of mathematical expertise.

span.label: contradicts → Hurford (ref. 7, p. 305), "without language, no numeracy"
span.quote: Amalric and Dehaene’s findings ( 1 ) suggest otherwise.

span.label: critiques → Hurford's claim that there is no numeracy without language
span.quote: Hurford famously stated: “without language, no numeracy” (ref. 7 , p. 305). Amalric and Dehaene’s findings ( 1 ) suggest otherwise.

span.label: supports → Amalric and Dehaene (2016), the commented paper
span.quote: In PNAS, Amalric and Dehaene ( 1 ) report data that significantly advance our understanding of the origins of high-level mathematical abilities.

span.label: supports → Dehaene and Cohen's prediction of a visual number form area
span.quote: In an influential neuropsychological model of number processing, Dehaene and Cohen ( 13 ) predicted the existence of a visual number form area (VNFA) in the ventral visual cortex.

span.label: critiques → the early structural studies of Einstein's brain
span.quote: However, the methodologies used to study the structure of Einstein’s brain have been subject to substantial criticism ( 3 ).

span.label: RETRACTED (RE-GROUNDED) · mathematical expertise —distinct-from→ language
span.quote: Notably, the brain regions found to be engaged by expert mathematicians during the reflection on mathematical statements lie outside areas typically associated with language.

span.label: symbolic number processing —part-of→ mathematical expertise
span.quote: These findings reveal a connection between the neural circuits engaged during elementary numerical processing and higher level mathematics.

span.label: nonsymbolic —distinct-from→ symbolic number processing
span.quote: A connection between symbolic numbers and mathematical expertise in the brain does not necessarily imply that the same is true for nonsymbolic number processing ( 9 ).

span.label: visual number form area —part-of→ ventral visual cortex
span.quote: In an influential neuropsychological model of number processing, Dehaene and Cohen ( 13 ) predicted the existence of a visual number form area (VNFA) in the ventral visual cortex.

span.label: visual number form area —operationalised-as→ inferior temporal gyri
span.quote: recent studies ( 15 ) using electrocorticography as well as novel methods for high-resolution fMRI ( 16 ) have revealed regions in the bilateral inferior temporal gyri that respond significantly more to numerical symbols compared with letters and other nonnumerical symbols

span.label: frontoparietal —part-of→ domain-general
span.quote: It is well established that the frontoparietal brain regions found to be engaged by expert mathematicians are associated with numerous cognitive processes that are not specific to mathematics, such as working memory, attention, and task difficulty ( 12 ).

span.label: Neurosynth —operationalised-as→ reverse-inference
span.quote: What is displayed in this figure are the results of a reverse-inference meta-analysis conducted using Neurosynth ( 6 ).

span.label: Neurosynth —operationalised-as→ numerical
span.quote: The brain activation displayed in orange corresponds to regions that are reported more frequently when an article mentions the term “numerical” in the abstract (taken from 89 studies) compared with articles that do not mention the term numerical.

span.label: RETRACTED (THE SPAN IS A PROHIBITION ON THE EXACT INFERENCE THE EDGE MAKES) · plasticity —causes→ ventral visual cortex
span.quote: Importantly, as Amalric and Dehaene ( 1 ) acknowledge, such correlational data cannot be used to infer causality.

span.label: functional connectivity —operationalised-as→ language
span.quote: or that such a relationship exists at the level of functional connectivity with language areas of the brain rather than through their direct recruitment

span.label: visuospatial skills —causes→ mathematical expertise
span.quote: Recent evidence has revealed that visuospatial skills fully explain

span.label: electrocorticography —contrasted-with→ functional magnetic resonance imaging
span.quote: Although functional neuroimaging studies were unable to support this prediction for many years ( 14 ), recent studies ( 15 ) using electrocorticography as well as novel methods for high-resolution fMRI ( 16 ) have revealed regions in the bilateral inferior temporal gyri that respond significantly more to numerical symbols compared with letters and other nonnumerical symbols.

span.label: recycled —causes→ symbolic number processing
span.quote: How exactly are the neural mechanisms underpinning elementary numerical processing bootstrapped or recycled ( 10 ) to give rise to mathematical expertise?

span.label: mathematical expertise —distinct-from→ language
span.quote: Although some have argued that language provides the basis for high-level mathematical expertise, others have contended that such mathematical abilities are linked to nonverbal processes that underpin the processing of magnitude and space.

span.label: meta-analysis
span.quote: What is displayed in this figure are the results of a reverse-inference meta-analysis conducted using Neurosynth

span.label: The author's own Neurosynth reverse-inference meta-analysis shows that brain regions associated with numerical processing are largely anatomically separate from those associated with language.
span.quote: This analysis provides support for the finding that the processing of numerical information is (largely) anatomically distinct from the brain circuitry that is thought to underpin linguistic functions.

span.label: The commentary concludes that the absence of language-area recruitment in expert mathematicians refutes the claim that high-level mathematical ability is grounded in language systems.
span.quote: By showing that expert mathematicians do not recruit brain areas associated with language when engaged in mathematical thinking, Amalric and Dehaene ( 1 ) refute the hypothesis that higher level mathematical abilities are grounded in language systems of the brain.

span.label: The commentary argues the overlap between advanced mathematical reflection and elementary number processing implies a deep continuity between rudimentary symbolic number skills and advanced mathematics.
span.quote: the data speak against the notion that basic number concepts have little to do with advanced mathematics and instead suggest a deep connection between rudimentary symbolic number processing and advanced mathematics

span.label: The author qualifies the refutation: language may still matter for the initial acquisition of expertise or through functional connectivity rather than direct recruitment.
span.quote: Notwithstanding, it is possible that language may have played a role in the initial acquisition of mathematical expertise or that such a relationship exists at the level of functional connectivity with language areas of the brain rather than through their direct recruitment.

span.label: The author raises an untested alternative account, that experts may simply attend differently to statements in their domain, and proposes a non-mathematical expert control group to separate domain-general attention from domain-specific processing.
span.quote: Nevertheless, it is possible that the mathematical experts attended differently to the mathematical statements because they are particularly salient to them.

span.label: The commentary cautions that the expertise-related differences in ventral visual cortex are correlational and cannot establish that training caused them.
span.quote: Importantly, as Amalric and Dehaene ( 1 ) acknowledge, such correlational data cannot be used to infer causality.

span.label: the author's own Neurosynth meta-analysis, run for this commentary, separates numerical from language regions across 89 and 885 studies
span.quote: The brain activation displayed in orange corresponds to regions that are reported more frequently when an article mentions the term “numerical” in the abstract (taken from 89 studies) compared with articles that do not mention the term numerical.

span.label: the commentary's reading: the language hypothesis for advanced mathematics is refuted, with two weaker forms left standing
span.quote: By showing that expert mathematicians do not recruit brain areas associated with language when engaged in mathematical thinking, Amalric and Dehaene refute the hypothesis that higher level mathematical abilities are grounded in language systems of the brain.

span.label: the commentary's open question: how elementary number circuits are recruited into expertise is not addressed by the data
span.quote: What Amalric and Dehaene’s findings ( 1 ) leave open is exactly how the connection between basic and higher level mathematics is constructed during the process of acquiring mathematical expertise.

span.quote: In an influential neuropsychological model of number processing, Dehaene and Cohen ( 13 ) predicted the existence of a visual number form area (VNFA) in the ventral visual cortex.
